enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B - COMPOSITION (40 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (12 marks); Expression (16 marks); Accuracy (12 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write on from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 450 - 500 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **e)** Write a story to illustrate the proverb: *Blood is thicker than water.*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: the proverb and the two brothers, Tanyi and Ayuk.
2. A family land dispute and false friends who turn Tanyi against his brother.
3. Tanyi falls into debt and is attacked; his friends vanish, his brother rescues him.
4. Reconciliation.
5. Moral: blood is thicker than water.

**Model composition (479 words)**

In my village, the elders say, "Blood is thicker than water," meaning that the bond between members of the same family is stronger than any other relationship. I understood this proverb fully through the story of two brothers, Tanyi and Ayuk.

Tanyi and Ayuk were the sons of a farmer in a small village in the North West Region. When their father died, he left them a large coffee farm to share. Ayuk, the elder, was quiet and hardworking. Tanyi, the younger, was lively and loved to be surrounded by friends. Soon after the burial, a quarrel arose over the boundary of the farm. A group of Tanyi's friends, who spent their days drinking in his compound, told him that Ayuk wanted to cheat him. "He is the elder, so he will take the best part," they said. "Leave the farm to us, and we will help you chase him away." Tanyi, who believed everything his friends told him, stopped speaking to his brother. The two men lived in the same compound as strangers.

Then came the dry season, and with it, bad luck. Tanyi sold his share of the farm to pay for expensive parties for his friends. They praised him, called him "chief" and ate and drank at his expense. Within months, the money was finished, and the friends disappeared one by one. Tanyi began to borrow money from a dangerous man in the market, who demanded his payment in two weeks.

When the day came, Tanyi had nothing. The man arrived with three strong youths, who dragged Tanyi into the compound and began to beat him. Tanyi cried out for help and called the names of his friends, but no one came. They had all gone to the town. His neighbours watched from a distance, afraid to interfere.

It was Ayuk who heard the cries from the farm. He ran home with his machete and stood between his brother and the men. "If you touch him again, you will deal with me," he said. The men were frightened and withdrew, and the next day, Ayuk sold part of his harvest and paid the debt in full. He then carried his bleeding brother to the hospital and sat beside his bed for three days.

When Tanyi opened his eyes and saw his brother, tears flowed down his cheeks. "Forgive me, my brother," he whispered. "I believed strangers more than my own blood." Ayuk held his hand and said, "You are my brother. There is nothing to forgive." They returned to the farm, worked together and planted new coffee trees. Tanyi never again sat with those who had abandoned him.

The villagers often tell this story to their children. It shows that friends may come and go according to our fortune, but a brother will stand by us in time of trouble. Truly, blood is thicker than water.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 12 | Relevant ideas that answer the topic, developed with examples, in clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 16 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate style and tone, fluent links between ideas |
| Accuracy | 12 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. A story with no clear link to the proverb, or a proverb that is only quoted and never illustrated by the events.
2. Telling the moral at the beginning and then repeating it.
